title: Garden Design

learn.summary: Good design is mostly logistics: put the garden where you see it daily (you tend what you see), near a water source, in your best sun. Start smaller than you think — a well-tended 4x8 bed outproduces a neglected quarter acre. Layout choices (raised beds, containers, vertical supports) are tools matched to your space and soil, not ideology.

do: Draw your garden to scale on graph paper (1 square = 1 foot), placing beds within 50 feet of a spigot and along a path you walk daily

children.title: Companion Planting

learn.summary: Some pairings have real mechanisms: flowers interplanted among vegetables draw pollinators and pest-eating insects, tall crops shade heat-hating lettuce, and legumes fix nitrogen. Much classic companion lore (carrots love tomatoes) is folklore with weak evidence, so treat charts skeptically. The reliably supported move is simply diversity — mixed plantings confuse pests better than monoculture rows.

do: Interplant a flower with known insectary value — sweet alyssum, calendula, or marigold — every 3-4 feet through one vegetable bed

children.title: Raised Beds vs In-Ground

learn.summary: Raised beds give you controlled soil, faster spring warm-up, better drainage, and no compaction from foot traffic — build them no wider than 4 feet so you can reach the center. In-ground rows are far cheaper and hold moisture better in hot climates. Choose raised beds for bad or contaminated soil and tidy small spaces; in-ground for scale and low budget.

do: Price out one 4x8-foot raised bed (lumber plus about 21 cubic feet of soil mix) against sheet-mulching the same footprint in-ground, and pick one to build this month

children.title: Container Growing

learn.summary: Containers grow real food on balconies and patios, but they dry out fast and leach nutrients with every watering — expect to water daily in summer heat and feed every 2-3 weeks. Bigger is easier: a 5-gallon container is the minimum for a tomato or pepper; herbs and lettuce manage in 1-2 gallons. Every pot must have drainage holes; use potting mix, never garden soil.

do: Plant one 5-gallon container (bucket with drilled holes works) with a pepper, cherry tomato, or herb trio in fresh potting mix

children.title: Vertical Growing

learn.summary: Trellised vines — pole beans, cucumbers, peas, indeterminate tomatoes — can triple production per square foot while improving airflow and keeping fruit clean and visible. A cattle-panel arch or netted A-frame handles most crops; heavy fruits like small melons need slings. Place trellises on the north side of beds so they do not shade shorter neighbors.

do: Install one trellis (bamboo teepee, netting, or cattle panel) on the north edge of a bed and sow pole beans or cucumbers at its base
